Previous studies show that teachers report feeling unprepared to integrate AI technologies pedagogically, citing limited training opportunities, insufficient insti- tutional support, and absence of clear competency frameworks (Kasinidou et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025). Although AI utilization is becoming widespread in education, teachers remain cautious due to concerns about ethical use and data privacy ([Alexandrowicz, 2024)](#5-conclusion). Additionally, the rigid boundaries of the curriculum and the lack of institutional support significantly limit educators' ability to effectively use AI technologies in their classrooms.

Improper use and misunderstanding of AI by teachers hinder their capacity to utilize it effectively and appropriately (Ng et al., 2025; Velander et al., 2024). These challenges underscore that enhancing AI literacy programs is vital to ensure educators can effectively implement AI tools in teaching practices (Kokoç et al., 2026; Cao et al., 2026; Sperling et al., 2024). The PD landscape reflects this fragmentation, ranging from brief technical workshops focused on tool operation to extended programs emphasizing critical pedagogical application. Un- derstanding which PD approaches effectively develops teacher AI liter- acy, and how these approaches might be adapted across diverse educational contexts, represents a critical knowledge need for the field.

### _1.1._ _Conceptual foundations: Defining and Delimiting AI literacy_

The concept of AI literacy has undergone considerable evolution over the past decade. Early formulations defined it primarily as a set of cognitive competencies enabling individuals to understand, use, and critically evaluate AI technologies (Long & Magerko, 2020; Ng et al., 2021). These initial conceptualizations were largely knowledge-oriented, emphasizing awareness of AI concepts such as machine learning, data representation, and algorithmic decision-making. Kong, Yang, and Hou (2024) extended this perspective by framing AI literacy as a multifaceted competency that encompasses not only conceptual understanding but also the capacity to apply AI across diverse contexts at home, at school, and in the workplace for collaboration, critical evaluation, and ethical problem-solving. They argued that AI literacy development should prioritize conceptual un- derstanding and active citizenship over narrow technical or program- ming skills. Following the public release of large language models like ChatGPT and the subsequent proliferation of GenAI tools in educational settings, the construct has expanded further. Since 2022, some studies have increasingly framed AI literacy as a multidimensional competence encompassing technical understanding, ethical reasoning, critical eval- uation of AI-generated outputs, and the capacity to integrate AI tools into domain-specific professional practices (Ng et al., 2025; Sperling et al., 2024). For in-service teachers specifically, this shift has meant that AI literacy is no longer reducible to knowing what AI is; it now entails pedagogical judgment about when, why, and how to deploy AI in ways that are educationally meaningful, ethically responsible, and contextually appropriate (Tan, 2025; Zhou et al., 2025).

The literature employs several related but conceptually distinct terms including AI literacy, AI competence, AI readiness, and technology acceptance/adoption often without clear differentiation ([Almatrafi et al., 2024;](#5-conclusion) Chiu, 2025). As Chiu et al. (2024) argue, literacy con- cerns what to know and what skills are needed, whereas competency relates to the ability to apply that knowledge effectively and with con- fidence. In this review, AI literacy is understood as the overarching construct that integrates knowledge, skills, and dispositions necessary for informed engagement with AI technologies in professional practice. AI competence, in this framing, refers to demonstrable performance capabilities in applying AI tools and can be considered a behavioral manifestation of literacy (Chiu et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025). AI readiness, by contrast, emphasizes perceived preparedness and will- ingness to engage with AI, often operationalized through attitudinal and motivational measures such as confidence, relevance perceptions, and anxiety (Ayanwale et al., 2022; Ramazanoglu ˘ & Akın, 2025). 

Technology acceptance and adoption, grounded in models such as TAM and UTAUT, focus on the psychological and contextual determinants of behavioral intention to use technology, and thus represent a distinct but intersecting theoretical tradition (Venkatesh et al., 2003). During the screening and selection process of the present review, studies were included if they explicitly addressed teachers' AI-related knowledge, skills, or competencies, regardless of the specific terminological label used. However, studies that examined technology adoption without any substantive engagement with AI literacy as a knowledge or competence construct were excluded. This conceptual positioning allows the review to capture the breadth of current research while maintaining analytical coherence around AI literacy as the central organizing construct.

### _1.2._ _Literature review_

Research on AI in education has expanded substantially over the past decade, leading to an increasing number of systematic reviews exam- ining AI applications, pedagogical affordances, and ethical consider- ations across educational contexts. Early large-scale reviews primarily focused on technological functions and system-level outcomes. For example, Zawacki-Richter et al. (2019) analyzed 146 studies published between 2007 and 2018 and identified profiling and prediction, assessment and evaluation, adaptive systems, and intelligent tutoring as dominant application areas. Their review also drew attention to the limited empirical focus on teachers and questioned their role in the implementation of AI in educational settings, indicating an early imbalance in the literature. Subsequent reviews have addressed more specific educational levels and stakeholder groups. These studies have documented instructional opportunities as well as ethical and practical challenges associated with AI-supported learning environments ([Alfarwan, 2025;](#5-conclusion) Crompton et al., 2024; Su et al., 2023). They asserted that teachers are most often positioned as implementers of AI-related practices rather than as professionals whose own competencies and learning processes are examined in detail.

Systematic reviews focusing on AI literacy and teachers in K–12 education further reinforce this perspective (Casal-Otero et al., 2023; Celik et al., 2022; Ng et al., 2025; Sperling et al., 2024; Tan, 2025; Tan & Tang, 2025). Casal-Otero et al. (2023), in a review of 179 studies, documented a rapid expansion of AI literacy initiatives at the curricular level but identified a persistent lack of coherent competency frameworks to support teachers' pedagogical use of AI, suggesting that instructional expectations often exceed available professional learning opportunities. Focusing specifically on secondary education, Ng et al. (2025) reported that teachers are frequently expected to implement AI-related content without sustained professional development or clearly articulated pedagogical and ethical competency frameworks, resulting in frag- mented practices and limited institutional support. Complementing these findings, Tan and Tang (2025), through a systematic review of empirical studies, highlighted that AI literacy research in K–12 educa- tion remains predominantly student-centered, with comparatively limited empirical attention to the development, assessment, and contextual conditions of teachers' AI literacy. Similarly, Tan (2025) emphasized that empirical studies continue to prioritize student out- comes, offering limited insight into how in-service teachers conceptu- alize AI, develop AI-related competencies, or integrate AI literacy into everyday instructional practice. Tan (2025) also highlighted the role of institutional factors, including professional development structures, policy guidance, and school-level support, while noting that these contextual dimensions remain insufficiently examined in existing syn- theses. Relatedly, Celik et al. (2022), in their systematic review of AI applications for teachers, identified a set of recurring challenges including limited pedagogical alignment of AI tools, insufficient pro- fessional development opportunities, and unclear expectations regarding teachers' roles that constrain teachers' effective engagement with AI in educational settings. Consistent with these observations, Sperling et al. (2024) conceptualize teachers' AI literacy as a situated 

and practice-oriented construct shaped by institutional conditions, pedagogical norms, and expectations associated with teacher profes- sionalism, underscoring the need to examine AI literacy development within teachers’ everyday professional contexts rather than as a set of decontextualized technical skills.

Within this body of review literature, in-service teachers occupy a distinct position. Unlike pre-service teachers, whose learning typically occurs within structured teacher education programs, in-service teach- ers are required to integrate AI into established pedagogical routines while responding to curriculum demands, assessment pressures, and school-level constraints. AI-related practices are embedded in profes- sional communities shaped by school culture, leadership support, and institutional expectations. However, existing review studies rarely examine how AI literacy is conceptualized, operationalized, and devel- oped among practicing teachers in relation to these contextual condi- tions. This limitation constrains understanding of how teachers interpret AI-related expectations and translate policy and curriculum discourses into classroom practice.

### _1.3._ _Motivation of the study_

Our systematic review addresses a critical gap in the literature by synthesizing empirical research that focuses specifically on in-service teachers’ AI literacy. While the field of artificial intelligence in educa- tion has generated a substantial body of research, existing syntheses rarely examine how teachers who are actively working in schools comprehend, develop, and enact AI literacy within their professional practice. Focusing on in-service teachers allows closer examination of the distinctive conditions shaping teacher learning, including the inte- gration of new competencies into established pedagogical routines, accountability and curriculum pressures, and constraints related to time and access to sustained PD. In line with these conditions, this review systematically examines how AI literacy is conceptualized and empiri- cally examined, the theoretical frameworks guiding research, the char- acteristics and reported outcomes of PD initiatives, and the ways AI is pedagogically integrated in studies focusing on in-service teachers. Accordingly, the current review addresses the following overarching research question: How is AI literacy conceptualized, theorized, devel- oped, and enacted in empirical research focusing on in-service teachers? This question is operationalized through three research questions that guide the analysis: 

**RQ1**. _How is in-service teachers' AI literacy conceptualized across empir-_ _ical studies, and which theoretical frameworks underpin this research?_

**RQ2**. _What are the characteristics, pedagogical designs, and reported outcomes of professional development programs targeting in-service teachers' AI literacy, including the integration of generative AI tools?_

**RQ3**. _What individual, psychological, and contextual factors are associ-_ _ated with in-service teachers' AI literacy, and how do these factors interact within institutional settings?_

Addressing these questions contributes to literature in several ways. The review provides a conceptually grounded synthesis that clarifies how AI literacy is defined and theorized in relation to in-service teach- ers, distinguishing it from adjacent constructs such as AI competence, readiness, and technology adoption. It also examines the design and effectiveness of PD initiatives, with particular attention to how gener- ative AI tools are incorporated into both instructional practice and research methodology. Furthermore, the review identifies the individual and contextual factors that shape teachers' AI literacy development within institutional settings, highlighting gaps and directions for future research in teacher education.

## 2. Method

A systematic review methodology was selected for this study because 

the research objective required a structured, replicable, and transparent approach to identifying, appraising, and synthesizing the available empirical evidence on in-service teachers' AI literacy. Unlike narrative reviews, which are more suited to broad theoretical discussions, or scoping reviews, which primarily aim to map the extent of research activity without appraising study quality (Munn et al., 2018), a sys- tematic review enables quality-assessed synthesis that supports evidence-based conclusions about what is known, where consensus ex- ists, and where gaps remain. The review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines (Haddaway et al., 2022) to ensure consistency, transparency, and replicability across all methodological stages. All procedures including search strategy, screening, quality assessment, and data extraction were predefined within the framework of the review protocol.

### _2.1._ _Search strategy_

A comprehensive database search was carried out in July 2025 using Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection. These two databases were selected because, together, they provide the most extensive coverage of peer-reviewed journals in educational technology, learning sciences, and teacher education, and their combined use is consistent with established practice in systematic reviews in this field (Crompton et al., 2024; Tan & Tang, 2025). While additional databases such as ERIC or PsycINFO might have captured further studies, prior methodological research has demonstrated substantial overlap between these sources and Scopus/Web of Science for educational technology topics (Martín-Martín et al., 2021), and the risk of missing relevant studies was mitigated by systematic reference-list checking during the screening process. The search was intentionally focused on "AI literacy" and "AI competence" as core descriptors. Adjacent terms such as "AI readiness," "AI integration," or "technology adoption" were not included as primary search terms, as these constructs, while related, stem from distinct theoretical traditions and would have substantially broadened the scope beyond the review's conceptual focus. During the screening process, however, studies retrieved through the primary search terms that sub- stantively addressed AI readiness or adoption in relation to teacher AI literacy were retained, provided they met the inclusion criteria outlined below:

TITLE-ABS-KEY ("ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE LITERACY" OR "AI LITERACY" OR "AI COMPETENC\*") AND TITLE-ABS-KEY ("TEACHER") AND (LIMIT-TO (DOCTYPE, "ar"))

The combined search produced 232 records (157 in Scopus and 75 in Web of Science). All records were imported into EndNote9, and dupli- cates were removed prior to screening.

### _2.2._ _Eligibility criteria and study selection_

Eligibility criteria were developed to capture empirical studies that directly addressed in-service teachers' AI literacy. To be included, studies needed to: (a) focus explicitly on teachers’ AI literacy, compe- tencies, knowledge, or skills; (b) involve in-service teachers working in K–12; (c) employ empirical methodologies (qualitative, quantitative, or mixed methods); (d) be published in peer-reviewed journals; (e) be written in English; and (f) be published between 2020 and 2025. The year 2020 was selected as the starting point because it marks the period when AI literacy began to be systematically conceptualized as a distinct educational construct in empirical research (Ng et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2025); and the subsequent years-particularly following the public release of ChatGPT in November 2022-witnessed a rapid increase in empirical activity. While this relatively short inclusion window limits the identification of longer-term trends, it was adopted deliberately to ensure that the reviewed studies reflect contemporary AI technologies and pedagogical contexts rather than earlier, pre-transformer-era research on general technology literacy.

Studies were excluded if they concentrated on students or pre-service 

teachers, assessed AI applications without addressing teacher literacy, included mixed groups without disaggregated teacher findings, lacked methodological detail, or represented non-empirical formats such as conceptual papers, reviews, or editorials. After removing 66 duplicates, 166 unique records proceeded to title and abstract screening, conducted independently by two trained reviewers. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion. This stage excluded 100 studies, leaving 66 articles for full-text review. Full-text assessment also conducted independently by two reviewers resulted in the exclusion of 23 additional studies due to insufficient teacher-specific data (n = 7), lack of explicit AI literacy focus (n = 5), absence of disaggregated results in mixed samples (n = 9), and insufficient reporting of essential methodological information, which precluded eligibility assessment (n = 2). A total of 43 empirical studies met all criteria and were included in the synthesis. The full process is illustrated in the PRISMA flow diagram ([Fig. 1)](#23-quality-assessment).

### _2.3._ _Quality assessment_

To ensure a rigorous evaluation of methodological quality across diverse designs, the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool 2018; Hong et al., 

**Fig. 1.**

2018\) was used. It enabled structured appraisal of five dimensions commonly emphasized in educational technology research: clarity of research questions, appropriateness of design, adequacy of sampling, validity of data collection procedures, analytic rigor, and transparency of reported findings and limitations. Two reviewers independently assessed 25% of the included studies (n = 11), demonstrating substantial inter-rater reliability (κ = 0.82). The remaining studies were evaluated by one reviewer with verification checks. No studies were excluded based on quality; instead, appraisal scores informed the interpretive weight assigned during synthesis. It should be noted that the two studies excluded during full-text screening for methodological reasons were removed at the eligibility stage due to insufficient reporting of essential methodological information, not as a result of MMAT quality scores. The MMAT appraisal was applied exclusively to the 43 studies that had already met all eligibility criteria, and no study was subsequently excluded on the basis of its appraisal results. Studies employing quan- titative survey designs generally demonstrated adequate sampling and validated instruments, though several relied on convenience sampling with limited sample sizes, which constrains generalizability. Among qualitative studies, transparency in reporting analytic procedures

varied. Mixed-methods studies were generally well-designed, though the integration of qualitative and quantitative strands was not always clearly articulated. These quality variations are reflected in the syn- thesis, where findings supported by methodologically stronger studies are given greater interpretive emphasis, while conclusions drawn pri- marily from studies with notable limitations are presented with appro- priate caution.

### _2.4._ _Data extraction_

A structured extraction form was created based on the review questions and piloted on five studies to refine categories. Extracted variables included bibliographic information, methodological charac- teristics (design, sample size, participant demographics, educational context), data collection and analysis methods, conceptualizations and operationalizations of AI literacy, measurement tools, theoretical frameworks, descriptions of AI tools or pedagogical contexts, PD pro- gram features (e.g., duration, format, learning activities), and reported challenges and key findings. To ensure reliability, two reviewers inde- pendently extracted data from 20 randomly selected studies (46.5% of the sample), producing strong agreement (κ = 0.85 for categorical variables; ICC = 0.91 for continuous variables). One reviewer completed the remaining extractions, and a second reviewer verified 25% for ac- curacy and completeness.

### _2.5._ _Data synthesis and analysis_

Given the heterogeneity of research designs, analytic approaches, conceptual frameworks, and reported outcomes, a narrative synthesis approach was adopted. Synthesis proceeded in three stages. First, a preliminary mapping of the included studies was conducted through descriptive tabulation, identifying patterns in methodological ap- proaches, sample characteristics, theoretical orientations, and AI liter- acy operationalizations. Second, thematic analysis was used to explore relationships among conceptualizations of AI literacy, measurement tools, PD characteristics, and pedagogical integration challenges. Third, the robustness of the synthesis was examined by comparing patterns across study quality levels, geographic contexts, and methodological types. To support interpretation, frequency distributions were generated for categorical variables (e.g., research designs, theoretical frame- works), and ranges were calculated for continuous variables such as sample sizes and PD program durations. These descriptive indicators complemented qualitative thematic analysis, enabling a comprehensive and integrative synthesis of the evidence. Findings were organized around the three research questions guiding the review, preceded by a descriptive overview of the included studies.

## 3. Results

This section presents findings from 43 empirical studies examining AI literacy among in-service teachers. It begins with a descriptive overview of the included studies, followed by findings organized around three research questions addressing conceptual and theoretical foun- dations, professional development programs, and factors associated with teacher AI literacy.

### _3.1._ _Descriptive overview of included studies_

The initial search across two databases yielded 232 records, of which 43 met all inclusion criteria. This relatively modest retrieval volume, combined with the fact that 93% of included studies were published in 2024–2025, suggests that empirical research on in-service teachers' AI literacy remains an emerging rather than saturated field, one that has gained rapid momentum following the generative AI surge but has not yet accumulated the critical mass needed for stable, cumulative con- clusions. Publication trends reveal dramatic recent growth in teacher AI 

literacy research. The temporal distribution demonstrates that 93% of included studies (n = 40) were published in 2024-2025, with only minimal earlier work (2023: n = 2, 4.7%; 2022: n = 1, 2.3%). This concentration reflects heightened scholarly attention following the November 2022 public release of ChatGPT and subsequent proliferation of generative AI tools in educational contexts. Geographic distribution is markedly uneven ([Fig. 2)](#33-rq2-professional-development-programs-and-genai-integration).

As seen in [Fig. 2,](#33-rq2-professional-development-programs-and-genai-integration) East and Southeast Asian contexts dominate the evidence base, with China (n = 13, 31.4%) contributing nearly one-third of studies. South Korea, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, the United States, Australia, and several European nations provide additional contribu- tions, while Africa, South America, and large portions of Europe remain substantially underrepresented. This geographic concentration raises questions regarding cross-cultural generalizability of findings and transferability of PD models across diverse educational systems. Meth- odological diversity characterizes the reviewed studies ([Fig. 3)](#33-rq2-professional-development-programs-and-genai-integration). As seen in [Fig. 3,](#33-rq2-professional-development-programs-and-genai-integration) quantitative approaches predominated (n = 17, 39.5%), primarily employing cross-sectional survey designs to assess AI literacy levels, attitudes, and technology acceptance ([Al-Amri & Al-Abdullatif, 2024;](#5-conclusion) Lin et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2022). Advanced analytical techniques included structural equation modeling to examine relationships among literacy constructs, affective variables, and behavioral intentions (Du et al., 2024; Kong, Korte, et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024), with partial least squares SEM accommodating smaller samples ([Al-Amri & Al-Abdullatif, 2024;](#5-conclusion) Ning et al., 2025). Three studies developed and validated new AI literacy instruments using confirmatory factor analysis (Chiu et al., 2025; Delcker et al., 2025; Younis, 2025). Qualitative studies (n = 12, 27.9%) examined teachers' experiences, perspectives, and implementation challenges through in- terviews and observations (Almuhanna, 2025; Kolemen ¨ & Yıldırım, 2025; Su, 2024). Mixed-methods approaches (n = 13, 30.2%) inte- grated quantitative and qualitative data through explanatory sequential designs (Kim & Kwon, 2023), parallel designs (Castro et al., 2025), quasi-experimental interventions (Kitcharoen et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2025), and design-based research (Brünner et al., 2025). Several studies demonstrated rigorous methodological triangulation (Chiu et al., 2024; Ramazanoglu ˘ & Akın, 2025), enhancing validity through multiple data sources and analytical approaches. Having established the descriptive landscape of the reviewed literature, the following sections address the three RQs guiding the current review study.

### _3.2._ _RQ1: Conceptualization and theoretical foundations of teacher AI literacy_

Fig. 4 presents an overview of the theoretical frameworks employed across the 43 studies included in the present study.

As the visual distribution indicates, the field does not rely on a single dominant framework. Rather, it draws upon several well-established models that collectively shape how teachers’ AI competencies, peda- gogical practices, and technology adoption processes are conceptual- ized. The reviewed studies draw most heavily on technology-adoption theories, with the Technology Acceptance Model (n = 7) constituting the most frequently applied framework, supplemented by UTAUT/UTAUT2, the Theory of Planned Behavior, and Social Cognitive Theory (n = 2). In parallel, a substantial proportion of studies employ pedagogical- integration frameworks, particularly TPACK and its AI-specific adapta- tions (each n = 5), together with sociocultural perspectives (n = 5), whereas competency-based frameworks such as DigCompEdu (n = 5) and the UNESCO AI Competency Framework (n = 1) are comparatively less represented.

The most frequently used frameworks belong to the technology- adoption category, with the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) appearing in multiple studies in various adapted forms. For example, Kolemen ¨ and Yıldırım (2025) examined preschool teachers' attitudes toward AI literacy using TAM, whereas Kong, Yang, and Hou (2024) employed an enhanced TAM structure to analyze teachers' behavioral

intentions toward AI-based learning environments. Likewise, the UTAUT2 model which synthesizes TAM with seven additional theoret- ical extensions, was used to explain teachers' adoption of AI-driven chatbots ([Al-Amri & Al-Abdullatif, 2024)](#5-conclusion). A second major cluster con- cerns pedagogical-integration frameworks, particularly the Technolog- ical Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) model. TPACK is widely used because it captures the interplay between technological, peda- gogical, and disciplinary knowledge, offering a multidimensional perspective on classroom-level AI integration. Both the classic TPACK model (Kim & Kwon, 2023; Wang et al., 2024) and contemporary ad- aptations such as AI Literacy TPACK and Intelligent-TPACK (Castro et al., 2025; Chiu et al., 2024; Velander et al., 2024) were applied to account for evolving teacher competencies in AI-supported learning environments. A third group centers on competency-based frameworks, most notably the UNESCO AI Competency Framework, which is frequently selected because it provides internationally recognized standards for situating teachers' AI literacy within a global policy context (Brünner et al., 2025; Pan & Wang, 2025; Zhao et al., 2022). In addition to these dominant frameworks, several supplementary theo- retical perspectives enrich the field, including Emotional Intelligence Theory, the Theory of Planned Behavior, Connectivism, Self-Determination Theory, Vygotsky's Sociocultural Theory, particu- larly the Zone of Proximal Development, Social Cognitive Theory, and the DigCompEdu framework. ### _3.3._ _RQ2: Professional development programs and GenAI integration_

A comprehensive analysis of the reviewed studies indicates that various types of PD initiatives (see Fig. 5) designed to enhance teachers’ AI literacy have expanded rapidly in recent years. As Fig. 5 illustrates, these initiatives vary substantially in structure, duration, and pedagog- ical orientation, with long-term structured programs and applied GenAI- focused training each representing 26.7% of all implementations, fol- lowed by short workshops (20%), school/government-led training (13.3%), and less frequent hybrid or co-design models (6.7% each). Among the 43 studies included in this review, 15 studies directly implemented AI-related training or PD programs for in-service teachers (see [Table 1)](#programs-typically-longer-in-duration-and-grounded-in-co-design-hands-on-application-or-iterative-reflection-eg-chiu-et-al-2024-34-rq3-factors-associated-with-teacher-ai-literacy-kong--yang-2024-xiao-et-al-2025-that-report-deeper-shifts-in), signaling a growing emphasis on systematic capacity building in this domain (Almuhanna, 2025; Brünner et al., 2025; Castro et al., 2025; Chiu et al., 2024; Davoodi, 2025; Kim & Rachmatullah, 2025; Kitcharoen et al., 2024; Kong & Yang, 2024; Moon et al., 2024; Ng et al., 2025; Park et al., 2023; Urazbayeva et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Wijaya et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2025).

According to the results of the studies, structured and application- oriented PD models appear to be particularly effective. For instance, a

Beyond PD program characteristics, the review also examined the extent to which GenAI tools were integrated into the research designs of the reviewed studies. The analysis shows that GenAI tools were rarely incorporated into the methodological core of research designs. The analysis of 43 studies shows that GenAI tools were rarely incorporated into the methodological core of research designs. Only three studies (7%) including Ng et al. (2025), Brünner et al. (2025), and Davoodi (2025) used GenAI tools in ways that intersected with their research procedures. [Table 2](#35-synthesis-of-overall-findings) presents these studies and the specific purposes for which the tools were used.

The first pattern concerns the support-oriented use of GenAI. In Davoodi (2025), GPT-4 contributed to the preparation of bilingual educational resources and administrative tasks during professional development. Its role, however, did not extend into data generation, analysis, or the construction of research instruments. A comparable situation is evident in Ng et al. (2025), where ChatGPT, Magic School, and Midjourney facilitated lesson planning, assessment design, content creation, and related instructional tasks. These tools shaped the peda- gogical environment of the study but did not influence how empirical evidence was collected or interpreted. A different level of integration appears in Brünner et al. (2025). ChatGPT (GPT-4o-mini) and the Col- lectiveGPT platform were embedded directly into workshop activities, where they supported prompt design, interactive learning tasks, and real-time comparisons between AI-generated and human responses. The tools were part of the instructional mechanism rather than peripheral aids. Even in this study, though, data analysis was conducted using standard statistical procedures, indicating a continued reliance on traditional methodological techniques despite the experimental use of GenAI within the intervention. The pattern across these studies illus- trates that the presence of GenAI remains concentrated in pedagogical or administrative functions, with limited penetration into methodological processes such as instrument design, coding, or analysis. GenAI tools have begun to influence the instructional components of research con- texts, yet their potential as analytical or methodological instruments is still largely unexplored within teacher AI literacy research.

synthesis of 43 studies reveals teachers AI literacy as a multidimensional construct shaped by interconnected cognitive, psychological, contex- tual, and organizational factors. The detailed findings from each indi- vidual study (N = 43) that inform this synthesis are elaborated in the comprehensive findings table presented in the Appendix**.** Despite considerable variation in theoretical grounding across educational set- tings, a cross-analysis of these studies identifies several convergent patterns. Taken together, these findings depict a field that is rapidly maturing yet remains marked by conceptual fragmentation, uneven methodological rigor, and significant systemic constraints. From a methodological quality perspective, findings related to the core triad of AI literacy components and the role of psychological mediators are supported by multiple studies that met most or all MMAT criteria, lending these conclusions greater confidence. In contrast, evidence regarding the sustained impact of PD programs on classroom practice remains limited, as even methodologically robust intervention studies (e.g., quasi-experimental and design-based designs) typically relied on immediate post-intervention assessments without longitudinal follow- up, warranting more cautious interpretation of long-term effectiveness claims.

A foundational pattern is the convergence on a core triad of literacy components: (a) technical knowledge concerning AI concepts, mecha- nisms, and applications (e.g., Kim & Kwon, 2023; Zhao et al., 2022); (b) pedagogical integration capacity, including the alignment of AI tools with instructional goals and assessment practices (Kong, Korte, et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024); and (c) ethical and socio-emotional compe- tencies, such as bias detection, data privacy awareness, and human-centered decision-making (Chiu et al., 2024; Velander et al., 2024). Studies examining teacher profiles (e.g., Pan & Wang, 2025; Wijaya et al., 2024) reinforce the robustness of these domains, finding that teachers with higher AI literacy consistently report stronger instructional alignment, more acute ethical discernment, and greater confidence in navigating AI-supported learning environments. Beyond these core components, the synthesis reveals the pivotal role of psychological mediators particularly self-efficacy, attitudes, trust, and emotional resilience as mechanisms that mediate the translation of knowledge into practice. Multiple studies employing structural equation modeling (e.g., Du et al., 2024; Ning et al., 2025) demonstrate that AI literacy alone is insufficient for behavioral adoption; rather, teachers’ confidence (i.e., self-efficacy) and perceived usefulness consistently predict actual integration. This suggests that advanced literacy requires not only technical competence but also a sophisticated reflective stance toward risks, ethical challenges, and pedagogical trade-offs. However, this interplay between literacy components and individual psychology is uniformly constrained by pervasive contextual and systemic factors. Findings highlight limited institutional support, insufficient training opportunities, unclear policies, and a lack of appropriate teaching re- sources across diverse geographic regions including Mainland China, Hong Kong, Saudi Arabia, Cyprus, and Europe (Castro et al., 2025; Kasinidou et al., 2025; Kolemen ¨ & Yıldırım, 2025). In early childhood and rural contexts, these barriers are amplified by infrastructural gaps, resource scarcity, and curricular misalignment. These patterns strongly suggest that teacher-level competencies must be supported by broader organizational and policy ecosystems if sustainable AI integration is to occur.

## 4. Discussion

This systematic review provides an integrated understanding of how in-service teachers’ AI literacy is conceptualized, measured, and devel- oped across 43 empirical studies published between 2020 and 2025. While AI literacy has rapidly emerged as a strategic priority in education systems worldwide, the findings reveal a field that is simultaneously expanding in scope and grappling with conceptual fragmentation, methodological imbalance, and significant contextual constraints. The rapid increase in research activity following ChatGPT's 

November 2022 release reflects both pedagogical urgency and techno- logical novelty (Tan, 2025). However, the significant concentration in East Asian contexts such as Mainland China, Hong Kong, and South Korea limits cross-cultural generalizability and underscores the need for comparative research in underrepresented regions such as Africa and Latin America, a pattern consistent with broader trends in AI education research (Nurgazina, Ravshanov, Usmanov, Ibragimov, & Sergeyeva, 2025). Methodologically, quantitative survey designs employing struc- tural equation modeling predominate (Arranz García et al., 2025), contrasting with growing calls for qualitative and design-based inquiries that capture teachers' contextualized experiences (Sperling et al., 2024). Nevertheless, emerging mixed-method and instrument-validation studies signal methodological maturation (Kokoç & Kara, 2021; Liu, 2025).

The theoretical architecture underpinning AI literacy studies reveals fragmentation rather than convergence, where diverse frameworks coexist with limited theoretical integration. Technology-adoption models (TAM, UTAUT) remain prominent, emphasizing perceived use- fulness and behavioral intention over pedagogical transformation (Zhao et al., 2025). This technocentric orientation likely stems from institu- tional pressures prioritizing adoption of metrics following the generative AI surge. In contrast to these adoption-focused frameworks, pedagogical models such as TPACK and its AI-specific adaptations (AI-TPACK, Intelligent-TPACK) mark a conceptual counterbalance that reframes AI not merely as a technological artifact but as part of teachers’ pedagog- ical reasoning, content representation, and instructional decision-making (Cao et al., 2026; Ning et al., 2024; Velander et al., 2024). The parallel rise of competency-based frameworks such as the UNESCO AI Competency Framework suggests a global policy turn, positioning AI literacy as a component of digital citizenship rather than a mere instructional innovation (Bai, 2025; Miao et al., 2024; Pan & Wang, 2025). Together, these theoretical pluralities reflect a transi- tional moment. As AI appears to be shifting from a technological novelty to a pedagogical paradigm, the field is moving from models explaining "_why teachers adopt AI_" toward frameworks exploring "_how teachers think and teach with AI_". However, this transition need not entail abandoning adoption perspectives altogether. Rather, a productive avenue for theoretical integration lies in recognizing that adoption and pedagogical frameworks address complementary dimensions of the same process. TAM and UTAUT explain what motivates teachers to engage with AI, including perceived usefulness, ease of use, and facilitating conditions, while TPACK and its AI-specific extensions explain how teachers inte- grate AI into their pedagogical reasoning and content knowledge. A conceptual bridge between these traditions would position AI literacy not as a static predictor of adoption intention, but as a dynamic pro- fessional competence that develops through iterative cycles of motiva- tion, experimentation, reflection, and pedagogical adaptation. Such a perspective aligns with the ecological view emerging from this review, where individual competencies, psychological dispositions, and insti- tutional conditions interact to shape teachers' AI literacy trajectories. Future research could operationalize this integrated perspective through longitudinal and design-based studies that trace how adoption-related motivations evolve into pedagogical expertise within specific school contexts.

Our study concluded that professional development initiatives designed to enhance teachers' AI literacy have expanded rapidly and diversified in structure and pedagogical orientation. Evidence from recent studies indicates that long-term, practice-oriented, co-design- based models yield substantial and sustained improvements in knowl- edge, confidence, and pedagogical skills (Lakhe Shrestha et al., 2025; Runge et al., 2025;), fostering professional agency and critical aware- ness ([Al-Amri & Al-Abdullatif, 2024)](#5-conclusion). Such approaches appear to enable teachers to move beyond instrumental use of technology toward trans- formative engagement with AI as a pedagogical partner. However, the current professional development landscape remains heterogeneous and theoretically fragmented. While some programs demonstrate robust 

design and evaluation frameworks, a considerable number of short-term or institutionally mandated initiatives focus primarily on tool familiar- ization with limited pedagogical depth, failing to produce sustained practice changes or critical ethical engagement (Barbieri & Nhu Nguyen Ruby, 2025; Tan, 2025). This pattern raises a fundamental question about whether current PD models primarily shift teachers' perceptions and self-reported confidence, or whether they generate the pedagogical expertise and institutional conditions necessary for lasting integration of AI into daily teaching routines. These inconsistencies reflect systemic challenges such as absent unified competency standards, insufficient policy alignment, and limited longitudinal evaluation opportunities. The emerging body of research points toward the necessity of integrated, theory-informed frameworks that combine technical skill acquisition with ethical reflection and context-sensitive pedagogy, conceptualizing AI literacy as multidimensional professional disposition rather than mere technical competence.

The results showed that teachers' AI literacy correlates strongly with self-efficacy, attitudes, and contextual variables. Within TAM and UTAUT2 frameworks, AI literacy functions as cognitive-affective construct, enhancing perceived usefulness, ease of use, and adoption intentions (Velli & Zafiropoulos, 2024; Zhao et al., 2025), with emotional intelligence mediating relationships between literacy and technology acceptance (Fu, 2025). These findings suggest that knowl- edge alone is insufficient without positive dispositions and affective readiness. It is important to note that high artificial intelligence literacy alone does not guarantee a smooth integration process. Contextual barriers such as infrastructure deficiencies, ethical concerns, and workload pressures limit the potential positive effects of literacy. This aligns with broader UTAUT2-based findings, which highlight that facilitating conditions and social dynamics often exert greater influence than cognitive variables alone ([Al-Amri & Al-Abdullatif, 2024)](#5-conclusion). These results highlight AI literacy as ecological construct shaped by in- teractions among self-efficacy, affect, and environmental affordances, necessitating research frameworks that move beyond predictive models of acceptance toward multidimensional approaches integrating psy- chological well-being, institutional support, and ethical sensibilities. These contextual dynamics are particularly salient for in-service teach- ers, whose AI literacy development is embedded in institutional realities that distinguish them from pre-service populations. Unlike student teachers learning within structured teacher education programs, prac- ticing teachers must negotiate AI integration alongside existing curric- ulum demands, accountability pressures, established collegial norms, and often limited discretionary time for professional learning. The reviewed studies consistently indicate that institutional factors including administrative support, school culture, access to infrastruc- ture, and policy clarity, function not merely as background conditions but as active determinants of whether individual AI competencies translate into sustained classroom practice. This finding underscores the need for future research to adopt workplace learning and organizational perspectives alongside individual competency models. Frameworks such as Activity Theory, which foreground the dynamic interplay among in- dividuals, mediating tools, and institutional contexts in shaping pro- fessional practice (Çakıroglu ˘ et al., 2016), could offer productive analytical lenses for examining how school-level structures enable or constrain teachers' AI literacy enactment.

Another important result is that teachers tend to use AI tools mainly for pedagogical and administrative purposes such as lesson planning, instructional design, and assessment support, rather than integrating them into the methodological foundations of educational research ([Alfarwan, 2025;](#5-conclusion) Barnes & Tour, 2025; Song et al., 2025). Barnes and Tour (2025) found that teachers often adopt GenAI tools informally to streamline routine tasks such as creating materials or adapting content for diverse learners, yet these practices rarely extend to systematic research engagement or data-driven innovation. Similarly, Song et al. (2025) reported that classroom integration of GenAI remains limited to facilitative roles, supporting instructional delivery rather than 

reshaping pedagogical inquiry or evidence generation. In a broader re- view of K–12 settings, [Alfarwan (2025)](#5-conclusion) concluded that while teachers recognize the efficiency and creative potential of GenAI, its use largely reinforces existing teaching practices instead of transforming method- ological approaches to educational inquiry. Even in cases where AI has been incorporated into research workflows, data analysis continues to rely on conventional statistical or interpretive methods, reflecting what Andersen et al. (2025) identify as the limited methodological impact of GenAI where its adoption enhances efficiency but seldom alters the underlying epistemic or analytical frameworks of research practice. Taken together, these findings suggest that while GenAI has begun to influence instructional innovation and practical aspects of educational research, its potential as a methodological agent capable of shaping how data are produced, analyzed, and theorized remains largely unrealized. This gap carries significant implications for the evolution of educational research methodology. As GenAI tools become capable of supporting qualitative coding, thematic pattern recognition, literature synthesis, and even hypothesis generation, their absence from research designs represents a missed opportunity for methodological innovation. Future studies could explore how GenAI might function not only as the object of inquiry but also as a research instrument, for instance, through AI-assisted analysis of classroom discourse, automated identification of pedagogical patterns, or collaborative human-AI coding procedures. Such integration would require careful attention to transparency, reproducibility, and ethical safeguards, but could substantially expand the methodological repertoire available to teacher education researchers.

Synthesizing across these dimensions, our review proposes that in- service teachers' AI literacy can be understood as operating at the intersection of three interacting layers: (a) an individual competence layer, comprising technical knowledge, pedagogical integration capac- ity, and ethical reasoning; (b) a psychological mediation layer, where self-efficacy, attitudes, trust, and emotional resilience shape whether and how competencies translate into practice; and (c) an institutional- contextual layer, including school culture, policy frameworks, infra- structure access, and PD structures, which enables or constrains both competence development and its enactment. This three-layer perspec- tive moves beyond the descriptive cataloguing of variables toward an integrative understanding of how teacher AI literacy develops and functions within professional practice. It also highlights a critical implication: interventions targeting only individual competencies, without addressing psychological readiness and institutional conditions, are unlikely to produce sustained change. The alignment between this layered perspective, UNESCO-oriented competency frameworks (Bai, 2025; Liu, 2025), and the ecological findings of this review suggests that future progress requires aligning teacher competencies with sup- portive institutional ecosystems through theoretically coherent models, context-sensitive methodologies, and policy-informed professional development.

## 5. Conclusion

This current systematic review of 43 empirical studies reveals that in- service teachers' AI literacy is an emerging but rapidly expanding research area marked by conceptual fragmentation and uneven institu- tional support. The three-layer perspective proposed in the study, inte- grating individual competencies, psychological mediators, and institutional-contextual conditions, offers a pathway beyond descrip- tive cataloguing toward a more theoretically grounded understanding of how teachers develop and enact AI literacy in practice. For policy and practice, the findings underscore that sustainable AI integration requires not isolated teacher training but coordinated efforts across competency development, psychological support, and institutional ecosystem building.

## 6. Limitations and future research

The present study is subject to several limitations. First, the scope was restricted to empirical studies published between 2020 and 2025, a deliberately short window that captures the period of rapid growth in this field but limits the ability to identify longer-term developmental trends or stable mechanisms. The concentration of 93% of included studies in 2024–2025 reflects the surge-driven nature of the current literature, and conclusions drawn from this corpus should be interpreted as indicative of an emerging field rather than as settled findings. Second, the search strategy focused on "AI literacy" and "AI competence" as primary descriptors. While this ensured conceptual coherence, it may have excluded relevant studies framed exclusively in terms of AI read- iness, AI integration, or technology adoption that did not use literacy or competence terminology. This lexical delimitation represents a trade-off between conceptual focus and comprehensiveness. Third, the focus on in-service K-12 teachers limits generalizability to pre-service teachers, higher education instructors, or informal learning contexts. Fourth, the exclusive inclusion of peer-reviewed journal articles may introduce publication bias, excluding grey literature and non-English studies that could provide important contextual insights. Future studies should broaden geographical coverage, employ more diverse methodological approaches (especially qualitative, DBR, and experimental designs), and incorporate psychological and sociocultural theories to capture the full complexity of teachers AI literacy. Additionally, as GenAI becomes embedded in instructional and administrative practices, studies should examine not only its pedagogical utility but also its role in shaping research design, ethics, and validity. Finally, there is a need for longi- tudinal and cross-cultural studies that trace how teachers’ AI literacy evolves across time, policy reforms, and technological change.
